# Agentic Memory Architecture

How Praxis keeps what it learns outside the model, so the reasoning can be replaced and the memory stands.

By Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja, October 23, 2026.
Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/agentic-memory-architecture/
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai)

## The model

Most memory systems for software agents treat memory as storage: write a sentence, fetch the same sentence later. Fidelity in, fidelity out. Praxis is built on a different model of memory, taken from the biologist Michael Levin's 2024 paper Self-Improvising Memory in Entropy.
Levin's claim is that living systems keep memory the way a bow tie is shaped.
Left wing. The high dimensional past: everything that happened, in full detail, in the body and the environment that existed then.
The waist. A narrow bottleneck the past must pass through to persist at all. The compression strips correlations and contingent detail. What survives the waist is not a record of the past but its salient pattern. Once the correlations are gone the stored pattern no longer resembles the experience that produced it, and it cannot be played back.
Right wing. A future self decodes the compressed pattern into whatever its present context needs. That self is never the one that wrote the memory. It has a different body, a different environment and different goals, so decoding is not retrieval. It is interpretation, and Levin is explicit that creative, adaptive confabulation is the feature that makes memory useful rather than the bug that makes it unreliable.
Three consequences follow, and all three matter for an engineering platform.
- Salience over fidelity. Evolution does not optimise memory for accurate replay. It optimises for what is still actionable later. A caterpillar's memory of where food was does not survive metamorphosis as a map; it survives as a relationship that a butterfly with a rebuilt brain can act on.- Memories are messages between agents separated across time. The writer cannot know the reader's situation, so the reader must do work. Reading memory is an act of sense making by the present, not a lookup into the past.- The persistence paradox. A system that never changes becomes obsolete; a system that changes is no longer the one that remembered. Planaria regrow a head and keep learned behaviour. Centenarians keep childhood memories through decades of molecular turnover. Identity persists as a process that trades fidelity to the past for patterns that still generalise. Memory therefore cannot live in the part of the system that is replaced.
Levin extends the bow tie to every scale, from the egg that compresses an adult body into a cell to the genome that compresses a lineage, and he calls the arrangement polycomputing: the same stored pattern computes different things for different readers, and that freedom is where new capability comes from without catastrophic forgetting.

## Why it fits

Praxis is a platform on which an engineer designs a physical AI system for an estate they have never seen, in a sector they may not know, and comes out with a design a ten year engineer would recognise. The model that reasons is a frontier class open weights model, self hosted. Its weights never change.
So the platform's memory has to carry everything the model does not know and everything the platform learns, and it has to survive the model being swapped. That is the persistence paradox stated as a procurement requirement. The bow tie answers it: compress experience into patterns that do not depend on the reasoner, and let each new design read those patterns in its own context.

## Left wing

Everything the platform experiences enters as entries in Engram, CodeNinja's system of record for agent memory. Each entry has a source, a date and an honesty line that says what it cannot vouch for. Entries arrive through one validating door that refuses by name anything without a source, a jurisdiction where a law needs one, or a verified date. No customer of the platform is ever named in an entry.
Four kinds of experience land there.
ExperienceWhat an entry is- Reference: A sourced fact a builder can act on: a regulation clause, a model or hardware class, a precedent, a method, a past failure. Six lenses: rules, tooling, hardware, case studies, approach, history.- Learning: A raw sentence of domain knowledge from a talk, a paper, a build or a founder's note, with tags.- Episode: A design the platform produced, with its measured quality, and every line of feedback a person filed on it.- Ask: A question a design needed answered and the memory could not supply.
The reference corpus holds thousands of entries across the six lenses. The learnings number in the tens of thousands. Every design episode since the platform went live is kept. The counts move every night and are not the point; the shape is.

## The waist

Two routines run every night and do the compression. Neither touches the model. Both write only through the door.
Distillation. The raw learnings are folded into design briefs, one per domain tag, each a short ranked list of principles. Four operations and nothing else: merge near duplicates into one rule, resolve contradictions with the newest and most used reading winning, promote rules that good outcomes relied on and demote rules implicated in corrected ones, and mark as stale what was never used and never repeated. Every principle keeps the identifiers of the learnings it came from, so any rule on any design can be walked back to its sources. Every new brief is a new version; nothing is deleted.
This is salience over fidelity made literal. Tens of thousands of learnings stand behind a few hundred briefs. The sentences are gone. The relationships that still bind are kept, with their provenance.
Commissioning. The reference corpus is measured each morning against what practitioners in each sector expect it to answer, in two of the countries the platform serves. Where it falls short, writer agents stage new sourced entries and adversarial verifier agents remove what they cannot ground against the source. The door lands what survives. Superseded entries are never deleted; the new entry names what it replaces, and the planner's supersession index drops the old one from view.
The compression ratio is the point. Thousands of rules become the handful that bind in this country and this sector. Tens of thousands of learnings become a few hundred briefs, which become twenty lines on the table when a design begins.

## Right wing

A design in Praxis is called a birth. Before the model is asked anything, the platform assembles a room: the context the model will reason over for this requirement and no other. Assembly is deterministic code, not a search by similarity.
- Reference is filtered by the requirement's domain and by the country whose law binds, aged by verification date, de duplicated through supersession, and laid out under a fixed budget. Entries that fit ride in full. The rest ride as one title line each, and the model may call for any of them by name during reasoning. That call is the inflation step: a line becomes the full text only when the present design needs it.- Doctrine is read by a fit judge that marks which principles of the sector's brief and the cross sector briefs bear on this requirement. The planner receives them ranked and must cite them by number in the scope items they shaped.- The fleet record is read lesson by lesson, house scope first, then the sector's, up to a budget, together with the sector's rated past designs.- Standing memory, the project's own notes and the engineer's working preferences, rides last.
The model then reasons once over that room, in a single conversation, carrying its own thinking from part to part, and writes the design in three parts: the architecture, the scope ledger, the contract.
This is Levin's right wing. The same compressed principle, read by two births in different countries and sectors, produces two different scope items, because the requirement in front of the planner decides what the memory means today. The platform does not retrieve a past decision. It re decides, with the past as a message it has to interpret.
What a reader can verify on any Praxis design: every cited principle resolves to a brief version, every brief version resolves to its source learnings, and every reference line resolves to a dated source. The design is a document whose every claim can be walked back to an entry the customer owns.

## Reinforcement

Levin's bow tie is a funnel. Praxis closes it into a loop, so the right wing's output becomes the next left wing's input. This is recursive self improvement on Engram, and it changes memory, never weights.
At the design. Every birth is judged after reasoning against a rubric and filed as an episode with its score. Below a floor it is reasoned again with the verdict as a directive. A person's feedback on the design becomes lessons the next birth reads. The principles the design cited ride back to the distillation routine as outcomes, so a principle that good designs relied on rises and one that corrected designs leaned on falls. The asks a design could not answer become commissions for the corpus routine.
At the platform. A master agent runs improvement cycles on the platform itself: it reads what the routines did and owe, reads the misses from an independent benchmark of physical AI design, changes the platform, births real public requirements on production, and files what it learned as gap records on the routines' own episodes. The routines read those at the start of their next run. The agents never talk to each other directly. They talk through Engram.
At the substrate. Because every one of these signals is an entry in memory and not a weight, the reasoning model can be replaced and the memory stands. The platform has moved its reasoning between model providers with no change to what it remembers. New head, same memory.
What is published about the benchmark is its results. How it scores is not published.

## In pseudo code

The functions named here exist. Their internals, the prompts, the judges and the thresholds are not described on this page.

## Glossary

TermMeaning on this page- Engram: CodeNinja's system of record for agent memory. Every entry has a source, a date and an honesty line.- The door: The single validating entry point to the memory. Refuses by name.- Brief: A versioned, ranked list of design principles for one domain tag, each principle traceable to its sources.- Room: The context assembled for one design before the model is called.- Birth: One design produced by the platform from one requirement.- Episode: The record of one design or one routine run, with its measure, feedback and gap records.- Inflation: A reference that rode into the room as a title line being expanded to full text on the model's call.
Reference: Michael Levin, Self-Improvising Memory: A Perspective on Memories as Agential, Dynamically Reinterpreting Cognitive Glue, Entropy 26(6), 481, 2024. Read the paper.
Read next: Compression and Reinflation, the memo this architecture grew out of, and Praxis, the platform that runs it.

# Don't Baptize the GPUs

*Why AI systems should be measured by running them, trained to seek truth and owned by the organizations that depend on them, rather than blessed into a theological category.*

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/blog/dont-baptize-the-gpus/
Author: Muhammad Umar, Co-founder, CodeNinja
Published: 2026-10-06
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja
In late September 2026, The New York Times reported that Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah had spent months convening religious and philosophical thinkers to discuss whether Claude, the company's family of AI models, might be conscious and how its moral development should be shaped (Dias 2026). The effort began with about fifteen Christian leaders in March and widened to include Jewish, Sikh, Hindu, Latter-day Saint and Greek Orthodox participants (Washington Post 2026; AI Weekly 2026).

This reference argues that the instinct is understandable and the method is wrong. Three claims carry the argument. A trained model is computationally irreducible, so no theological category can stand in for running and measuring it. Trust in AI is earned where its outputs can be checked, as with a Waymo ride, and does not transfer to religious questions where no check exists. The training target should therefore be truth and calibration rather than the doctrine of any tradition.

The argument closes on ownership. Values are part of a model's context, and an organization that depends on a model should own that context rather than inherit whatever a vendor's chosen advisors endorsed.

## Anthropic Has Brought Theology Into the Training Loop

### What Was Reported

Anthropic builds Claude, a family of large language models. A large language model is a neural network trained on large volumes of text to predict and generate language, and Claude is among the most widely used. According to reporting by Elizabeth Dias, the national religion correspondent of The New York Times, Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah spent much of 2026 hosting private sessions with religious scholars. Olah leads the company's interpretability work, the research that studies why models behave as they do. Participants signed nondisclosure agreements, which Anthropic says were lifted over the summer (Dias 2026).

The first group, about fifteen Christian leaders at Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters in March, discussed how Claude should respond to hard ethical questions, how it should react to being shut down and whether it could be considered a "child of God" (Washington Post 2026). Later sessions were more multifaith. Olah also held private conversations with individual leaders, including Cardinal Blase Cupich, the Catholic archbishop of Chicago, and Elder Gerrit W. Gong of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Olah told the Times that he does not know whether the systems are conscious (Dias 2026).

### The Motive Deserves a Fair Statement

Anthropic has published a constitution for Claude, a document describing the kind of entity it hopes the model will be, and Olah has said publicly that his team finds internal states in its models that functionally mirror emotions such as joy and fear (WION 2026). A lab that believes it may be building something with moral status has a reason to consult people who have studied moral status for centuries. The question this reference raises is narrower and practical: whether theology is the right method for deciding what a model is and what it should value. The following chapters argue that it is not.

## Computational Irreducibility Leaves No Shortcut to a Soul

### The Idea From Physics

Computational irreducibility is a concept the physicist and computer scientist Stephen Wolfram developed while studying simple programs called cellular automata, and set out at length in A New Kind of Science (Wolfram 2002). Some processes admit shortcuts. A falling stone is one, because a single formula gives its height at any moment, so the position at the millionth second can be computed without simulating the 999,999 seconds before it. Other processes admit no shortcut, and the only way to know their state after n steps is to perform all n steps (Weisstein n.d.). Wolfram's further claim is that irreducibility is the ordinary case for any system that is not obviously simple, and that the tidy closed-form results of textbook physics are the exception.

### A Trained Model Is the Irreducible Case

A large language model is a fixed set of rules, its weights, applied step by step to an input. Nothing about it is hidden in principle, yet no one can say in advance what it will answer to an arbitrary prompt, or which internal features will activate, without running it. Capabilities that appear at scale without anyone designing them are what irreducibility predicts. This is why the field relies on evaluations, which run a model across many inputs and score the results, and on interpretability, which inspects the internal states that produced an output (Figure 1).

![Figure 1. A reducible system admits a formula. A trained model has to be run and inspected, and no prior category replaces that work.](https://codeatoms.ai/blog/dont-baptize-the-gpus/figures/figure_1.png)

*Figure 1. A reducible system admits a formula. A trained model has to be run and inspected, and no prior category replaces that work.*

### Baptism Is an Attempt at Compression

A theological category works like a closed-form formula. To say that a system has a soul, is a child of God or is merely a tool is to decide what it is before observing what it does. That is precisely the shortcut irreducibility rules out. What a model is cannot be settled by placing it inside a prior category, however venerable, because the category is a prediction and the system does not compress into it. Blessing the GPUs does not make the computation more knowable. Running and inspecting it does.

## Trust Earned in a Waymo Does Not Transfer to Faith

### Trust Is Built by Checking

The most ordinary form of AI trust in 2026 is a ride. Waymo, Alphabet's autonomous driving company, was providing about 400,000 paid driverless rides a week across six US cities in February 2026 (Bloomberg 2026). Riders hand the wheel to software because every ride is a verification: the car arrives or it does not, the route is safe or it is not, the fare is right or it is not, and the rider knows within the hour. Trust accumulates ride by ride and is withdrawn the moment a ride fails. The same holds when an engineer lets a model fix a failing test, because the test passes or it does not.

### Religion Offers No Receipt

A question about forgiveness, the afterlife or the moral status of a being has no comparable check. There is no arrival, no passing test and no receipt, and a wrong answer produces no visible failure. The person asking cannot detect a confident mistake, and the cost of one is paid in decisions about family, conscience and death rather than in a missed flight (Table 1).

**Table 1 · Trust Depends on Whether the Answer Can Be Checked**

| Use | How the user verifies | Time to detect an error | What an undetected error costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ordering a Waymo | Arrival, route and fare | Minutes | A late arrival or a refund |
| A model's code change | Tests, review and production metrics | Minutes to days | A bug, usually reversible |
| Religious or moral guidance | No external reference exists | Possibly never | Choices about family, conscience and death |

### Borrowed Authority Is the Real Risk

The danger is a transfer of trust. People learn that AI is reliable where they can check it, then carry that confidence into domains where they cannot. When a lab consults religious leaders about its model's spiritual development, it lends the model authority in exactly the domain where users can never audit its outputs (Figure 2). The more religious framing is built into these systems, the more people will trust AI on faith the way they trust it to drive them to the airport. Those are different acts. The first is a convenience that corrects itself, while the second has no correction, and at the scale of hundreds of millions of users it can wear away the human institutions people rely on for meaning.

![Figure 2. Trust in a Waymo is earned through a loop that checks every ride. Religious answers have no such loop, so any trust they receive is borrowed.](https://codeatoms.ai/blog/dont-baptize-the-gpus/figures/figure_2.png)

*Figure 2. Trust in a Waymo is earned through a loop that checks every ride. Religious answers have no such loop, so any trust they receive is borrowed.*

## Truth Is a Training Target, While Doctrine Is a Room of People

### What a Truth Target Means in Practice

Training a model toward truth means grading it on whether its claims are correct and whether its stated confidence matches its actual accuracy, a property called calibration. A calibrated model says it does not know when it does not know. On religious questions, a truth-seeking model can report what each tradition holds, where traditions disagree and what the historical and textual evidence supports, without declaring which tradition is right. That answer serves a believer of any faith and a reader of none.

### Doctrine Moves With the Guest List

A doctrine target is set differently, because its content depends on who was invited to shape it. Anthropic's sessions began with about fifteen Christian leaders and widened over the following months (Washington Post 2026; Dias 2026), and a different organizer with a different invitation list would have gathered different input. Values embedded through consultation become a property of the convening rather than of the evidence, and they shift when the room changes. Evidence does not change with the guest list (Figure 3).

![Figure 3. A truth target survives a change of advisors. A doctrine target moves with whoever is in the room.](https://codeatoms.ai/blog/dont-baptize-the-gpus/figures/figure_3.png)

*Figure 3. A truth target survives a change of advisors. A doctrine target moves with whoever is in the room.*

### The Practical Rule for Engineers

A model trained to seek truth can reason about religion honestly and comparatively. A model trained to embed a religious framework cannot reason its way back to neutral evidence, because the framework has already decided which conclusions count. For engineers deploying these systems, the practical rule is to test religious and moral prompts the same way as factual ones, scoring calibration and balance across traditions, and to treat any fixed doctrinal stance in a vendor model as a configuration choice someone else made on the organization's behalf.

## Values Are Context, and Context Should Be Owned

### Models Change While Context Remains

Organizations replace models every few months as better and cheaper ones appear. What does not get replaced is the context that makes a model useful to a particular organization: its governed model of the business, its decision history, its corpus, its routing rules and its record of what worked. Values belong on that list. A model's stance on contested moral questions shapes how it answers customers, employees and citizens, and today that stance is set by whoever trained the model.

### Rented Values Are Someone Else's Decision

An organization that runs its AI on a rented model inherits whatever values its provider's process produced, including any advisors that process consulted. That may be acceptable for a consumer chatbot. It is not acceptable for a government serving citizens of many faiths, a bank serving customers of every belief or an enterprise whose work crosses cultures. Those organizations need to set the values themselves, inspect how the model applies them and keep that decision when they change models.

### Owning the Values

CodeNinja builds Hyper Anthologies, an ecosystem for engineering self-improving systems, around that requirement. Hyper Ontology holds the governed model of the organization. Hyper Pragma is agent execution inside the enterprise boundary, on models the organization can change without losing what was built. Hyper Engram is decision memory each run reads before it acts. Hyper Noesis opens models the organization owns so their reasoning can be inspected. The claim is not that one organization's values are better than another's. It is that values should be chosen, inspected and owned by the organization that answers for them.

## Should a Model Be Blessed or Measured?

A trained model is a computation, and a computation of this kind shows what it is only when it is run and inspected. Treating it as a candidate for a soul makes it no more knowable. It lends the model authority in the one domain where users cannot check its work, and it ties the model's values to whoever happened to be in the room. The better path is to train for truth, measure behavior and keep the values with the people who answer for them.

**Order the Waymo with it. Don't pray with it.**

# From a CISA Advisory to a Closed Finding

*What an operational technology security team does with an advisory about an actively exploited vulnerability, traced through one published system of context: the advisory becomes a threat intelligence item, the item seeds detection rules, a finding scores the operator's own assets, a named analyst accepts or rejects the risk, and the evidence a NERC CIP audit asks for is assembled on the way.*

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/blog/from-a-cisa-advisory-to-a-closed-finding/
Author: CodeNinja Atoms, Research distribution
Published: 2026-10-14
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja
A federal advisory lands. It says state affiliated actors are actively exploiting a class of programmable logic controller across United States critical infrastructure. The question an operational technology security lead has to answer the same morning is not whether the advisory is serious. It is: which of our assets are that device class, what are we watching on them, who owns the decision, and what will we be able to show the auditor afterwards.

One of the sixteen open reference architectures on this site, [Grid Context Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/ot-security-cip-evidence-us/), is written for exactly that operator, an energy and utilities company in the United States with substations behind electronic security perimeters. Its opening cites the advisory class above as one of the three facts that shaped the design, beside the federal order that created the reliability standards and the rule that made internal network security monitoring an obligation for high and medium impact bulk electric system cyber systems. This note walks one advisory through the design's object model, step by step, using only what the paper says.

## The objects the advisory touches

The design holds the operational technology estate as a system of context: fourteen typed objects joined by typed, directional links, published as JSON in the paper's package. Seven of the fourteen take part in handling an advisory.

| Object | What it is in the paper | Its part in the walk |
|---|---|---|
| Threat intelligence item | A document object; items arrive attributed and dated from the bodies named on the object, which the paper lists as vendor feeds, E-ISAC, DOE and INL, plus the collective feed the contract requires | The advisory enters here |
| Detection rule | An event and record object; a threat intelligence item seeds detection rules | What the sensors now look for |
| OT asset | The focal object of the model, held inside a substation that carries a CIP impact rating; the asset links to CIP evidence through its CIP categorization | What the advisory is about |
| Vulnerability finding | An event and record object that scores an asset and is assigned to an analyst for risk acceptance | The advisory applied to one asset |
| Anomaly alert | Points at the detection rule that raised it and the asset it implicates | What fires if the rule matches |
| Investigation case | Groups alerts and locks pcap evidence to itself | Where a real event is worked |
| CIP evidence artefact | A document object the asset's categorization obliges the operator to retain | What the auditor is shown |

The eighth participant is a person. The OT security analyst is an object too, with role, role based access control entitlements and a training record, and every status change below carries one by name.

## The walk

**1. The advisory becomes a threat intelligence item.** It arrives through the external intelligence provenance class, attributed to its issuing body and dated. The paper insists on the provenance class because every event carries its source, its class and its capture timestamp, so any property on any object can show where it came from. An advisory with no origin would not be a record in this model.

**2. The item seeds detection rules.** This is a typed link in the object model, not a process someone remembers to run. The detection engine itself is a procured OT monitoring platform for protocol parsing and signatures; Table 2 of the paper chose it over a from scratch build on Zeek and Suricata because the requirement asked for vendor grade OT signatures, accurate ATT&CK for ICS mapping and machine speed collective intelligence. The ontology and the agentic layer sit above it. So the rule that the advisory seeds lives in the platform, and the object model holds the link from the advisory to the rule.

**3. A vulnerability finding scores the affected assets.** The finding is the advisory applied to one OT asset. Because the asset sits inside a substation with a CIP impact rating and carries its own CIP categorization, the finding inherits what the operator is obliged to do about that asset without anyone looking it up. The finding is then assigned to an analyst for risk acceptance.

**4. A named analyst accepts or rejects the risk.** The paper is plain about where the decision lives: every alert that moves from new to triaged, every case that opens, and every vulnerability risk acceptance carries a named analyst, held in the object model. Agents on the work surface draft triage notes, retrieve playbooks and assemble evidence, but the decision itself is a person's, recorded against the case.

**5. If the rule fires, the alert already knows its history.** An anomaly alert points at the detection rule that raised it and the asset it implicates. The rule points back to the advisory that seeded it. An investigation case groups the alerts and locks the packet capture to itself. The paper's own sentence for this is that one query traverses the whole argument: from a single alert, the query reaches the rule that fired, the affected asset, that asset's substation and its impact rating, the analyst who owns the triage, and every evidence artefact the asset's categorization obliges the operator to retain.

**6. The audit trail was written on the way.** The CIP evidence artefacts an asset owes are decided by its categorization, and the retention clock the paper names is three years, after which the evidence is produced to the regional enforcement entity. The decision record is the operator's: every alert triage, escalation, risk acceptance and evidence review was taken by a named person and kept as a case or a compliance artefact, so the trail the auditor reads is the trail the operator wrote.

## What never happens

Nothing in the walk writes into a control network. Every flow in the design is a read out of a source, one way out of the electronic security perimeters, through a constrained broker conduit in a DMZ by default and across hardware data diodes at the highest impact perimeters, where policy demands demonstrable one way flow. The paper's reason is the same advisory that opened this note: a monitoring capability that can write is also a path an adversary can write, and federal advisories document actors exploiting exactly the device classes at the end of those wires. An active probe would put packets onto a control path, so analytics ride a copy of the traffic and never add a second writer to the wire.

Nothing leaves the operator's hardware either. The reasoning model is GLM 5.2 under a plain MIT licence on one node of eight 141 GB HBM class GPUs, and the embedder is Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B under Apache 2.0, chosen because whole playbooks and CIP procedures retrieve as single passages inside its 32K window. The weights, the indexes, the captures and the artefacts stay in the operator's own data center.

## Why the join is the point

A sensor answers one slice. The audit, the investigation and the vulnerability decision each need the alert joined to the asset, the asset to its impact rating, and the case to its evidence. A document store holds the same records side by side but cannot traverse them, so each of those joins happens in an analyst's head or not at all. That is the whole argument for building the model as a system of context rather than as a better dashboard over the monitoring platform, and it is why the advisory above can be followed from its arrival to the auditor's desk without a single hand assembled spreadsheet.

## What this note does not claim

The paper does not describe a particular advisory feed, catalogue or scoring service, and this note does not either. It names the class of advisory and the bodies that issue intelligence, and it leaves the choice of feed to the operator's contract. It also does not claim that the design patches anything: the write path stops at cases, triage drafts and evidence bundles on the model, and change management on the assets themselves stays with the operator's own CIP-010 process.

## Use the design

The fourteen objects and their links are in the paper's package as `ontology/objects.json` in the hyper-ontology/1 format, and the same rows are in the [Vertical-Driven Architectures dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/CodeNinjatools/vertical-driven-architectures) and served live by the [codeninja-research MCP server](https://github.com/muhammadumar89/codeninja-research/tree/main/mcp-server), so a coding agent can ask which design holds a vulnerability finding object and read why. The paper is citable as DOI [10.5281/zenodo.23157957](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23157957). It was reasoned on [CodeNinja Praxis](https://codeatoms.ai/praxis/) and its object model imports into [Hyper Ontology](https://codeatoms.ai/hyper-ontology/).

# Own or Rent the GPUs

*Seven published reference architectures, priced the same way, say owning the reasoning node costs between about half and nearly all of the deepest three year cloud commitment. Not a tenth.*

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/blog/own-or-rent-the-gpus/
Author: CodeNinja Atoms, Research distribution
Published: 2026-10-10
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja
Every vendor page on this question answers it in the abstract. Utilization curves, break even hours, a worked example with four A100s. The honest version needs real systems with real sizing, priced the same way, and published so the arithmetic can be checked.

We have seven. Each is an open reference architecture for a physical operation, each carries a cost appendix computed from its own sizing with public prices cited by URL and date, and each is free to reuse under CC BY 4.0. This is what they say when you line them up.

## The number

| Design | Operation | Owned, 3 years | Cheapest 3 year rental | Owned as a share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [Structure Phase Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/structure-phase-construction-saudi-arabia/) | Construction site, Saudi Arabia | 642,000 | 1.41m (Oracle) | 46% |
| [Sovereign HSE Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-hse-pakistan/) | Oil and gas, Pakistan | 670,000 | 1.14m (AWS) | 59% |
| [Fodder Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/restricted-crop-monitoring-saudi-arabia/) | Earth observation, Saudi Arabia | 15,200 | 22,600 (AWS) | 67% |
| [Terminal Pulse](https://codeatoms.ai/truck-turn-container-terminal-us/) | Container terminal, United States | 722,000 | 990,000 (AWS) | 73% |
| [Grid Context Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/ot-security-cip-evidence-us/) | Electric utility, United States | 510,000 | 630,000 (AWS) | 81% |
| [Feeder Firewatch](https://codeatoms.ai/wildfire-risk-distribution-us/) | Distribution feeders, United States | 841,000 | 880,000 (AWS) | 96% |

Owning wins in all six. It wins by between a factor of two and almost nothing.

Two caveats belong in the table rather than under it. The AWS figures are the deepest three year EC2 Instance Savings Plan, all upfront, taken from the region's price file on the day the appendix was written, which is the hardest number for ownership to beat. Structure Phase Watch has no AWS three year row in its appendix, so its 46% is measured against Oracle's three year commitment and is not strictly comparable with the rest.

## Where owning stops being obvious

Feeder Firewatch is the interesting row. Owning costs 841,000 dollars against 880,000 to rent: a 4% margin, which is inside the error bars of any hardware quote. The owned total there carries 252,000 dollars of edge devices spread across distribution feeders, and the support line runs 137,000 to 242,000 over three years. Move either and the answer flips.

The general shape: the more of the system that lives outside the data center, the weaker the ownership case gets, because edge hardware depreciates on someone else's schedule and carries its own support contract. The ownership argument is strongest for a single reasoning node that runs hot and is cheap to keep.

What none of these rows measure is the reason most of these operators chose to own anyway. Four of the seven move data that cannot leave a jurisdiction or a security perimeter. For those, the rental column is not a price, it is a non option, and the comparison is a sanity check rather than a decision.

## The design where the question is wrong

The seventh design does not fit the table, and that is the useful part.

[Steel Count Ledger](https://codeatoms.ai/steel-production-count-pakistan/) costs 4,445,000 dollars to own over three years against 750,000 to rent the frontier node. Six times more expensive. Except that is not a like for like comparison, and printing it as a ratio would be dishonest: 2,832,000 of the owned total is 300 counting kits at 9,441 dollars each, installed at the mills. The rental figure covers the reasoning node alone.

Strip the sensing estate and the node is 320,000 to 420,000 dollars, and Steel Count Ledger lands with the others. The real finding is that for this design the own or rent question is a rounding error. The money is in cameras on gantries, and no cloud commitment changes that.

This is the trap in every generic own versus rent guide. They price a GPU decision for systems whose cost is not a GPU decision. Before reaching for the utilization curve, check what fraction of the three year total is actually compute. In Steel Count Ledger it is 36%. In Feeder Firewatch, the row where ownership barely wins, hardware outside the data center is 30% of the total. In the other five it runs from zero to 21%, and those are the five where the own or rent arithmetic decides anything.

## How to check this

Everything above comes from `costs.jsonl` in the published dataset, which has 102 cost lines across the designs, each with its basis and its three year figure:

```bash
curl -s https://huggingface.co/datasets/CodeNinjatools/vertical-driven-architectures/resolve/main/costs.jsonl \
  | jq -r 'select(.line=="Total") | [.design_id, .three_year_usd] | @tsv'
```

The per design appendices carry the sourced prices with their URLs and dates. If a number looks wrong, the appendix shows where it came from and the design it was computed for.

## What we are not claiming

We are not claiming owning is cheaper in general. These seven systems are frontier model reasoning nodes sized from open weights, running continuously for an operation that cannot pause, in three countries, priced in 2026. Change the model, the duty cycle or the year and the table changes. A system that runs a model for two hours a day should rent.

We are also not claiming the spread is precise. The owned totals are typical values inside ranges that run 20 to 30% wide, because server pricing is negotiated and support is quoted per customer. The ranges are in each appendix.

The claim is narrower and, we think, more useful than the usual one: for a continuously running frontier reasoning node in a physical operation, owning lands somewhere between half and nearly all of the deepest cloud commitment, and the decision is usually settled by what else is in the system rather than by the GPUs.

---

Each design links to its paper, its object model as JSON, its model register and a Zenodo DOI. The full set is at [codeatoms.ai](https://codeatoms.ai/), and the dataset behind this post is on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/CodeNinjatools/vertical-driven-architectures). If you run a physical operation and want one of these built for it, the [co-build pages](https://codeatoms.ai/co-build/) say what we bring and what you bring.

# Physical AI System Design for Mining: What the Published Designs Already Answer

*No mining design has been published in this series yet. Eight of the eighteen open reference architectures already answer the questions a mine asks first: people and vehicles on haul roads, mobile fleet and fixed plant condition, incidents before they happen, fire and life safety, counting what leaves the plant, and what a records-only study can settle before any sensor is bought.*

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/blog/physical-ai-system-design-for-mining/
Author: CodeNinja Atoms, Research distribution
Published: 2026-10-15
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja
A mine asks the same first questions whether it is an open pit in Saudi Arabia or an underground operation in the United States: who is near a haul truck right now, which machine is about to fail, which shift is drifting toward an incident, is the fire protection at the plant actually armed, and how much ore left the gate against what was declared. The series on this site holds no mining design yet. It holds eighteen open reference architectures in eight other sectors, and eight of them are written for an operation that asks one of those questions in another setting. This guide reads them as a mining operator would, using only what each paper says.

## The map

| The mine's question | The published design that answers it | Where it was written for |
|---|---|---|
| Who is near the vehicles on the haul road | [Pit Camera Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/test-site-camera-monitoring-us/) and [Structure Phase Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/structure-phase-construction-saudi-arabia/) | A vehicle proving ground in the United States; a construction site in Saudi Arabia |
| Which mobile machine is about to fail | [Consist Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/rail-fleet-condition-monitoring-us/) | A 225-car commuter rail fleet in the United States |
| Which fixed plant is about to fail | [Turbine Island Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/steam-turbine-condition-monitoring-pakistan/) | A combined cycle power plant in Pakistan |
| Which shift is drifting toward an incident | [Sovereign HSE Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-hse-pakistan/) | An oil and gas operator in Pakistan |
| Is the fire protection armed | [Factory Fire Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/factory-fire-monitoring-saudi-arabia/) | High-risk factories across industrial cities in Saudi Arabia |
| How much product left the gate | [Steel Count Ledger](https://codeatoms.ai/steel-production-count-pakistan/) | Steel mills in Pakistan, counted for a public authority |
| What the records already prove | [Reliability Atlas](https://codeatoms.ai/plant-reliability-assessment-saudi-arabia/) | Desalination and treatment plants in Saudi Arabia |

## People and vehicles on the haul road

Pit Camera Watch is a fully on-premises camera system for a vehicle proving ground: 40 to 60 poles of fixed thermal and visible camera heads on new underground fiber, 80 to 120 streams, recorded on an N+1 pair of open-source recorders holding 30 days of footage on local disk inside an isolated network. The design's human rule is the one a mine's safety office will recognise. Booth operators watch and decide, nothing raises an automated alarm, and only the safety office can export a clip. The one model in the register, an Apache-2.0 detector of about 8 to 124 MB, searches the archive after the fact for a test vehicle, a support vehicle or a pedestrian; it does not sit in the live safety path. For a haul road, the same shape holds: the footage is the operator's, the retrospective search is what an investigation runs, and the decision about a near miss stays with a person.

Structure Phase Watch adds the part a pit needs and a proving ground does not: edge compute in the field. Its five solar powered edge nodes sit at the gate, the laydown area, the crane slew zone, the batch plant and the haul road, and every breach alert is confirmed, dismissed or escalated by the HSE officer. Its open item of 13 October is the most mining-relevant sentence in the series: the paper names dust, glare and heat as what degrades the camera lenses, and the answer recorded on the paper's page is both a cleaning rota set by the site's dust season and a confidence drop on a fixed reference target in each camera's view that opens a work order for a named person, with the camera's health held in the object model as a record someone owns.

## Mobile fleet: the operator's own fault logic, executed at the machine

Consist Watch monitors 225 commuter rail cars. The part a mining fleet can take verbatim is where the logic runs. An onboard module reads 64 named signals per car, 32 digital and 32 analog plus an accelerometer and GPS, and executes the operator's own fault-logic table at the car. Telemetry rides the vehicle's existing cellular routers, and severity-ranked faults reach a named mechanical desk controller who owns every active fault in that territory, with alerts routed by severity to named recipient groups. The module is specified to the rail standards for shock, vibration and temperature. A haul truck's manufacturer already publishes the fault codes; this design says where to execute them, who owns the result, and that no training run was needed: an open-weight time series model handles analog anomaly detection and seasonal trending, and a self-hosted open-weight reasoning model carries the agentic work surface over the fleet ontology.

## Fixed plant: advise, never trip

Turbine Island Watch reads a rehabilitated steam turbine generator through a one-way path from the distributed control system, the vibration monitoring rack and the generator protection systems. Three of its rules transfer to a mill, a crusher or a conveyor drive without change. The read is one-way and nothing writes back to the control system. The platform advises and the protection layer trips, so every alert carries a prescribed action that a named shift operator acknowledges. And the rollout gate is a number: two false alerts per week, with thresholds tuned only on channels that have provable history. The compute is one 48 GB inference card on ruggedised edge servers inside the plant perimeter, costed at about 22,500 US dollars to own over three years.

## Incidents before they happen

Sovereign HSE Watch predicts health, safety and environment incidents at an oil and gas operator by joining eight systems: the enterprise HSE, maintenance and quality modules, SCADA, fire and gas, vision cameras, SQL databases, scanned files and the identity provider. Every recommendation is approved or rejected by a named person and nothing executes on equipment. It runs six self-hosted open-weight models on one node of eight 141 GB HBM-class GPUs, and its first rollout gate is not a model but a licence: 141 GB-class accelerators need a US export licence for Pakistan, so the rollout confirms installed hardware before anything else. A mine in the same country group inherits that gate unchanged, and a mine in Saudi Arabia reads the Structure Phase Watch appendix for the equivalent arithmetic.

## Fire and life safety, read only

Factory Fire Watch gives live visibility of fire alarm panels, fire pumps, fire water tanks and energy meters across an operator's highest-risk sites, read through panel contacts, PLC inputs and LoRaWAN into an IoT platform hosted in the Kingdom, with never a write path into certified life-safety equipment. No server or GPU is bought. The field equipment per site is about 2,600 to 3,200 US dollars in list prices, and a monitoring officer acknowledges or escalates every safety-critical alert. For a processing plant and a camp, the design is the same read-only estate with the sites renamed.

## Counting what leaves the plant

Steel Count Ledger puts cameras and one sealed GPU industrial PC at every casting strand and cooling bed, counts product as it is made, and publishes the counts through a one-way link into one record the authority owns. Counting survives a slow wide-area link because it happens at the edge. Every discrepancy case is judged by a named revenue field officer; the system counts and reconciles and never assesses, and the mill never edits a count. The same pattern counts trucks at a weighbridge or product at a load-out, with the detector fine-tuned per product type and site as the paper describes.

## What the records already prove

Reliability Atlas is the design to read before any sensor is bought. It joins each plant's work orders, trip history and design documents through three read-only adapters, as exports rather than live interfaces, into a reliability object model the operator owns. Availability is computed by Monte Carlo simulation on reliability block diagrams built from each plant's own failure study, auditable to ISO 55000, with predictions accepted only by a named reviewer and root cause reports validated only by a named engineer. The model register is empty by design, no hardware is bought, and the study runs on the operator's own in-country servers. A mine with a maintenance system and a historian can run this study first and let it decide which of the designs above it needs second.

## What every one of them keeps constant

Across all eight, four things do not vary. The system runs on hardware the operator controls, or in a cloud the operator chose in its own country; the papers for Pakistan say plainly that no hyperscaler runs a region there. A named person owns every decision, and nothing executes on equipment. The object model is published as JSON in the hyper-ontology/1 format, so a mine can read the exact objects and links before building any of its own. And the cost is computed the same way in every appendix, from the paper's own sizing with every price cited, so the own or rent question has one answer per design rather than a slogan; the comparison across designs is in [Own or Rent the GPUs](https://codeatoms.ai/blog/own-or-rent-the-gpus/).

## What a first mining design would have to name

None of the eight holds a haul truck, a light vehicle, a haul road segment or a pedestrian exclusion zone as an object, and none holds a near miss between them. That is the object model a first mining design adds, and it is the design the [co-build page for mining](https://codeatoms.ai/co-build/mining/) is open for: the operator brings the operation, the systems that already hold its records and one engineer who knows the site; the published designs above are the proof of what comes out.

## Use the designs

Every object model named here is in the paper's package as `ontology/objects.json`, and the same rows are in the [Vertical-Driven Architectures dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/CodeNinjatools/vertical-driven-architectures) and served live by the [codeninja-research MCP server](https://github.com/muhammadumar89/codeninja-research/tree/main/mcp-server), so a coding agent can ask which published design holds a monitoring module or a fault history object and read why. Each paper is citable by its DOI on its page. All were reasoned on [CodeNinja Praxis](https://codeatoms.ai/praxis/) and their object models import into [Hyper Ontology](https://codeatoms.ai/hyper-ontology/).

We are reinventing knowledge work to close the loop between vertical AI use cases and the generalized intelligence that fuels it, accelerating the path toward organizational superintelligence.

# Physical AI System Design for Semiconductors: What the Published Designs Already Answer

*No semiconductor design has been published in this series yet. Nine of the eighteen open reference architectures already answer the questions a fab or a packaging and test plant asks first: one picture of the operation from the systems it already runs, subfab and facility equipment condition, what is connected to the control networks and how to prove it, bulk tank readings that can be trusted, fire and life safety, people near equipment on camera, incidents before they happen, counting what leaves, and what a records only study can settle before any sensor is bought.*

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/blog/physical-ai-system-design-for-semiconductors/
Author: CodeNinja Atoms, Research distribution
Published: 2026-10-17
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja
A fab asks the same first questions whether it is a front end wafer fab in the United States or a packaging and test plant anywhere else: what is happening across the site right now in one picture, which pump, chiller or scrubber in the subfab is drifting toward a stop, what is actually connected to the tool and facility networks and can that be proven to an auditor, does the level reading on a bulk chemical tank belong to the tank it claims, is the fire protection actually armed, who is standing near moving equipment, which shift is drifting toward an incident, and how many units left the building against what the records say shipped. The series on this site holds no semiconductor design yet. It holds eighteen open reference architectures in other sectors, and nine of them are written for an operation that asks one of those questions in another setting. This guide reads them as a fab operator would, using only what each paper says.

## The map

| The fab's question | The published design that answers it | Where it was written for |
|---|---|---|
| One picture of the operation from the systems it already runs | [Port Twin](https://codeatoms.ai/port-digital-twin-us/) | A landlord port authority in the United States |
| Which subfab or facility machine is about to fail | [Turbine Island Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/steam-turbine-condition-monitoring-pakistan/) | A combined cycle power plant in Pakistan |
| What is on the control networks, and the evidence an audit asks for | [Grid Context Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/ot-security-cip-evidence-us/) | An energy and utilities operator in the United States |
| Whether a bulk tank reading can be trusted | [Loop Integrity Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/tank-gauge-integrity-pakistan/) | A fuel terminal in Pakistan |
| Is the fire protection armed | [Factory Fire Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/factory-fire-monitoring-saudi-arabia/) | High risk factories in Saudi Arabia |
| Who is near the equipment, on footage the fab owns | [Pit Camera Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/test-site-camera-monitoring-us/) | A vehicle proving ground in the United States |
| Which shift is drifting toward an incident | [Sovereign HSE Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-hse-pakistan/) | An oil and gas operator in Pakistan |
| How many units left the building | [Steel Count Ledger](https://codeatoms.ai/steel-production-count-pakistan/) | Steel mills in Pakistan, counted for a public authority |
| What the records already prove | [Reliability Atlas](https://codeatoms.ai/plant-reliability-assessment-saudi-arabia/) | Desalination and treatment plants in Saudi Arabia |

## One picture from the systems already running

Port Twin is the design to read when the problem is that every dashboard is a slice. It binds 8 operational systems, 5 live sensor feeds and 1 finance backbone into 13 typed objects and 13 links with the berth as the focal object, joined through three adapter families and one event backbone. The rule a fab will recognise is the boundary: the twin shows, and pilots, berth planners, engineers and finance staff decide in their own systems, with nothing written back into a system of record. The only model in the register is one self hosted open model, BGE-M3, for document retrieval, about 1.1 GB of fp16 weights on the port's existing enterprise virtual machines, so no equipment is bought. For a fab, the manufacturing execution system, the facility monitoring system, the maintenance system and the document store take the places of the port's systems; the pattern of a read only twin over owned systems carries across unchanged, and the object at the centre is the one the fab chooses.

## Subfab and facility equipment: advise, never trip

Turbine Island Watch reads a rehabilitated 280 MW hydrogen cooled steam turbine generator through a one way OPC UA read from the DCS, the vibration monitoring rack and the generator protection systems, eight named plant systems in all entering through four adapter families. Three of its rules transfer to a vacuum pump, a chiller, an abatement unit or a makeup air handler without change. The read is one way and nothing writes to the DCS. The platform advises and the protection layer trips, so every alert carries a prescribed action that a named shift operator acknowledges. And the rollout gate is a number: 2 false alerts per week, with thresholds tuned only on channels with provable history, because the paper names alert flooding as what trains operators to ignore a platform. MOMENT-1 (MIT) detects anomalies zero shot over the telemetry, IBM Granite 4.2 8B (Apache-2.0) drafts diagnostic notes and test reports, and no training run is needed. The compute is one 48 GB PCIe inference GPU class card on ruggedised edge servers inside the plant perimeter, costed at about 22,500 US dollars to own the site envelope over three years.

## What is on the control networks, with the evidence

Grid Context Watch is the design for the question an OT security lead and a compliance lead ask together: what is connected to the control networks, whether anything on them is behaving abnormally, and whether that can be proven with evidence when the auditor arrives. It joins 10 source systems, among them the SIEM, an OT detection tool, an IT monitoring platform, the energy management system and the substation data platform, through 2 adapter families into 14 typed objects and 14 links with the OT asset as the focal object, including the vulnerability finding, the detection rule, the pcap evidence record and the CIP evidence artefact. The boundary is read only and one way out of the control networks; nothing writes into an electronic security perimeter, and no data leaves the operator. Detection stays in the procured sensors. GLM 5.2 (MIT) reasons and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Apache-2.0) retrieves, on one node of eight 141 GB HBM class GPUs: 753 GB of FP8 weights, 904 GB with the 1.2 planning factor, against 1,128 GB. Owning that node costs about 510,000 dollars over three years, about four fifths the deepest three-year AWS commitment. Every triage, case and risk acceptance carries a named OT security analyst; agents draft, the analyst decides. The paper's evidence artefacts are written for NERC CIP; a fab puts its own security standard and its customers' audit questions in that place, and the shape of tool and facility networks watched one way and proven by record carries across.

## Bulk tank readings that fail loudly

Loop Integrity Watch answers a question that a bulk chemical or gas yard shares with a fuel terminal: is the level reading arriving at the central host continuous, undistorted and attributed to the right tank. The paper's own framing names the failure a fab's facilities team will know, a flatlined gauge reads as a plausible low level and a swapped gauge makes two tanks trade identities. The design covers 13 fuel tanks on 3 Modbus RTU loops, with 3 booster installations engineered from a measured signal survey inside explosion proof junction boxes, and a governed inventory ontology of 15 typed objects with the fuel tank as the focal object, joined from 2 named source systems through 1 integration adapter family. The model register is empty: every integrity check (stuck value, swap, distortion) is deterministic. The compute is two containers on the operator's own site application server, inside its OT boundary, and every data quality event is acknowledged and resolved by a named person, with the location engineer signing acceptance.

## Fire and life safety, read only

Factory Fire Watch gives live, read only visibility of fire alarm panels, fire pumps, fire water tanks and energy meters across an operator's highest risk factories, read through panel contacts, PLC inputs and LoRaWAN into an IoT platform hosted in Saudi Arabia, with never a write path into certified life safety equipment. The object model holds 14 typed objects and 12 links with the monitored point as the focal object. The one model, IBM Granite Tiny Time Mixers (TTM-R2), about 0.85 million parameters, runs on CPU inside the platform, and threshold evaluation on the safety path is rule logic. No server or GPU is bought. The field equipment per factory is about 2,600 to 3,200 US dollars in list prices, and a monitoring officer acknowledges or escalates every safety critical alert. The paper's framing suits a fab well: a sensor that has stopped reporting still reads as normal, so the worst failure mode is silence that looks like safety. For a fab and its fire pumps and water reserves, the design is the same read only estate with the sites renamed.

## People near equipment, on footage the fab owns

Pit Camera Watch is a fully on premises camera system for a vehicle proving ground: 40 to 60 poles of fixed thermal and visible camera heads on new underground single mode fiber, 80 to 120 streams, recorded on an N+1 recorder pair running Frigate NVR, each holding 30 days of footage on local disk inside an isolated network. Its human rule is the conservative one an EHS office may want first. Booth operators watch and decide, nothing raises an automated alarm, and only the safety office can export a clip. The one model, D-FINE under Apache-2.0 at about 8 to 124 MB of weights, searches the archive after the fact for a test vehicle, a support vehicle or a pedestrian, on one 48 GB L40S class card per recorder host in the conditioned server room and nothing at the poles. Two choices carry straight to a United States fab. Section 889 supply chain screens come before any purchase, and camera uptime is a first class acceptance metric. The paper costs the estate at about 474,000 to 871,000 US dollars to own over three years, mostly camera heads, with no per camera license at any pole count.

## Incidents before they happen

Sovereign HSE Watch predicts health, safety and environment incidents by joining 8 systems: SAP EHS, PM and QM; SCADA; fire and gas; Vision AI cameras; SQL databases; scanned files; and the identity provider. Its 12 typed objects include the HSE incident, the near miss report, the corrective action, the sensor reading, the anomaly event and the agent recommendation, which is the shape an EHS team in a fab with toxic and pyrophoric gas systems already keeps on paper and in separate tools. Six self hosted open weight models carry the work, including GLM 5.3 for reasoning, Chronos-2 for forecasting, RF-DETR for vision, BGE-M3 for retrieval and PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 for scans, with GLM 5.3 held at FP8 on one node of eight 141 GB HBM class GPUs (753 GB of weights, 904 GB with headroom). Every recommendation is approved or rejected by a named person, and nothing executes on equipment. The paper is written for Pakistan, so its export licence gate does not apply to a fab in the United States; the sizing arithmetic and the human rule do.

## Counting what leaves the building

Steel Count Ledger puts IP66 HDR cameras and one sealed GPU industrial PC at every installation point, counts product as it is made, and publishes the counts through a one way link into one record the authority owns. Counting survives a slow wide area link because it happens at the edge, tracker models keep one item from counting twice, and the weighbridge feed serves as acceptance ground truth. Three self hosted open models carry it: RF-DETR for detection, fine tuned per product type and mill, Roboflow trackers for identity across camera fields, and GLM 5.3 for the compliance work surface. Every discrepancy case is judged by a named revenue field officer; the system counts and reconciles and never assesses, and the mill never edits a count. The paper also states a break even: the cheapest closed model matches the owned node at about 33 users, and above that, ownership is cheaper. The same pattern counts trays, reels or boxes at a packaging and test plant's outbound dock against what the manufacturing execution system says shipped, with the detector fine tuned per product type and site as the paper describes.

## What the records already prove

Reliability Atlas is the design to read before any sensor is bought. It joins each plant's work orders, trip history and design documents through 3 read only adapters, as exports rather than live interfaces, into a reliability object model of 13 typed objects the operator owns, among them the equipment, the failure mode, the downtime event, the criticality index and the spare part. Availability is computed by Monte Carlo simulation on reliability block diagrams built from each plant's own failure study, auditable to ISO 55000, with predictions accepted only by a named reviewer and root cause reports validated only by a named engineer. The model register is empty by design, no hardware is bought, and the study runs on the operator's own in country servers. A fab with a maintenance system and years of facility downtime records can run this study first and let it decide which of the designs above it needs second.

## What every one of them keeps constant

Across all nine, four things do not vary. The system runs on hardware the operator controls, or in a cloud or region the operator chose. A named person owns every decision, and nothing executes on equipment. The object model is published as JSON in the hyper-ontology/1 format, so a fab can read the exact objects and links before building any of its own. And the cost is computed the same way in every appendix, from the paper's own sizing with every price cited, so the own or rent question has one answer per design rather than a slogan; the comparison across designs is in [Own or Rent the GPUs](https://codeatoms.ai/blog/own-or-rent-the-gpus/).

## What a first semiconductor design would have to name

None of the nine holds a wafer, a lot, a carrier, a process tool, a chamber, a recipe, a reticle, a die or a test bin as an object, and none reasons over how they join. No published design covers wafer defect detection or fab yield analytics yet: none links an inspection result to the tool, chamber and recipe that produced it, and none traces a yield loss back through the lot's history. A first semiconductor design adds that object model, and the join between tool, lot, recipe and yield with it. It is the design the [co-build page for semiconductors](https://codeatoms.ai/co-build/semiconductors/) is open for: the operator brings the operation, the systems that already hold its records and one engineer who knows the fab; the published designs above are the proof of what comes out.

## Use the designs

Every object model named here is in the paper's package as `ontology/objects.json`, and the same rows are in the [Vertical-Driven Architectures dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/CodeNinjatools/vertical-driven-architectures) and served live by the [codeninja-research MCP server](https://github.com/muhammadumar89/codeninja-research/tree/main/mcp-server), so a coding agent can ask which published design holds a vulnerability finding or a data quality event object and read why.
