# Physical AI System Design for Supply Chain and Logistics: What the Published Designs Already Answer

*No supply chain design has been published in this series yet. Eight of the eighteen open reference architectures already answer the questions a logistics network asks first: one picture across the nodes from the systems they already run, gate and yard turn time, whether a terminal's inventory reading can be trusted, which vehicle in the fleet is raising a fault, what is connected to the control networks at each site, counting what moves, incidents before they happen, and what a records only study can settle before any sensor is bought.*

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/blog/physical-ai-system-design-for-supply-chain-and-logistics/
Author: CodeNinja Atoms, Research distribution
Published: 2026-10-19
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja
A logistics network asks the same first questions whether it runs terminals and distribution centers in the United States or a fuel and freight corridor in Pakistan: what is happening across every node right now in one picture, why the trucks at the gate are waiting, whether the inventory a terminal reports is the inventory it holds, which vehicle in the fleet is about to fail, what is connected to the control networks at each site and can that be proven, how much moved against what the records say moved, and which site is drifting toward an incident. The series on this site holds no supply chain design yet. It holds eighteen open reference architectures in other sectors, and eight of them are written for an operation that asks one of those questions at a single node. This guide reads them as a network operator would, using only what each paper says. A guide for the building itself, the warehouse and its docks, aisles and conveyors, is [Physical AI System Design for Warehousing and Intralogistics](https://codeatoms.ai/blog/physical-ai-system-design-for-warehousing/); this one reads the network between the buildings.

## The map

| The network's question | The published design that answers it | Where it was written for |
|---|---|---|
| One picture across the nodes from the systems they already run | [Port Twin](https://codeatoms.ai/port-digital-twin-us/) | A landlord port authority in the United States |
| Why the trucks at the gate and yard are waiting | [Terminal Pulse](https://codeatoms.ai/truck-turn-container-terminal-us/) | A container terminal in the United States |
| Whether a terminal's inventory reading can be trusted | [Loop Integrity Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/tank-gauge-integrity-pakistan/) | A fuel terminal in Pakistan |
| Which vehicle in the fleet is raising a fault | [Consist Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/rail-fleet-condition-monitoring-us/) | A 225 car commuter rail fleet in the United States |
| What is on the control networks at each site, and the evidence an audit asks for | [Grid Context Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/ot-security-cip-evidence-us/) | An energy and utilities operator in the United States |
| How much moved, counted independently | [Steel Count Ledger](https://codeatoms.ai/steel-production-count-pakistan/) | Steel mills in Pakistan, counted for a public authority |
| Which site is drifting toward an incident | [Sovereign HSE Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-hse-pakistan/) | An oil and gas operator in Pakistan |
| What the records already prove | [Reliability Atlas](https://codeatoms.ai/plant-reliability-assessment-saudi-arabia/) | Desalination and treatment plants in Saudi Arabia |

## One picture across the nodes

Port Twin is the design to read when the problem is that every dashboard is a slice. It binds 8 operational systems, 5 live sensor feeds and 1 finance backbone into 13 typed objects and 13 links with the berth as the focal object, joined through three adapter families and one event backbone. The rule a network operator will recognise is the boundary: the twin shows, and pilots, berth planners, engineers and finance staff decide in their own systems, with nothing written back into a system of record. The only model in the register is one self hosted open model, BGE-M3, for document retrieval, about 1.1 GB of fp16 weights on the port's existing enterprise virtual machines, so no equipment is bought. For a logistics network, the transport management system, the warehouse management systems, the telematics feed and the finance system take the places of the port's systems; the pattern of a read only twin over owned systems carries across unchanged, and the object at the centre is the one the network chooses, a shipment, a load or a lane.

## Gate and yard turn time

Terminal Pulse predicts truck turn time two hours out at a container terminal and watches the yard live. The paper's own numbers frame the problem every gate office knows: turn time averages 54 minutes and spikes above 90, and the causes live in separate systems, so planners stitch them together at the morning and afternoon operations meetings and a spike is explained hours after the trucks felt it. The design joins eleven systems, among them the terminal operating system, the gate system, two crane management systems, reefer monitoring, railroad switch lists, cameras and weather and tide feeds, into twelve objects that include the truck visit, the gate lane, the yard block and the transfer zone. Five self hosted open models carry the work: GLM 5.3 for reasoning, Chronos-2 for forecasting, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B for retrieval, and RF-DETR with Roboflow trackers for vision. Two choices transfer directly to a distribution center's yard or a cross dock gate. The first rollout gate proves or redirects the yard side hypothesis using gate OCR data the operator already holds, before anything else is built. And the surfaces warn and propose while the named planner acts inside the terminal operating system; write back into that system is a second phase option gated on labour and IT sign off. The owned stack is costed at about 722,000 US dollars over three years. The operator in this paper is an illustrative scenario, not a customer.

## Terminal inventory that fails loudly

Loop Integrity Watch answers a question every bulk terminal in a fuel or chemical supply chain shares: is the level reading arriving at the central host continuous, undistorted and attributed to the right tank. The paper names the failure an inventory planner will know, a flatlined gauge reads as a plausible low level and a swapped gauge makes two tanks trade identities, and either one sends a wrong number into every replenishment decision downstream. The design covers 13 fuel tanks on 3 Modbus RTU loops, with 3 booster installations engineered from a measured signal survey inside explosion proof junction boxes, and a governed inventory ontology of 15 typed objects with the fuel tank as the focal object, joined from 2 named source systems through 1 integration adapter family. The model register is empty: every integrity check (stuck value, swap, distortion) is deterministic. The compute is two containers on the operator's own site application server, inside its OT boundary, and every data quality event is acknowledged and resolved by a named person, with the location engineer signing acceptance.

## Fleet faults: the operator's own logic, executed on the vehicle

Consist Watch monitors 225 commuter rail cars, and the part a truck, trailer or locomotive fleet can take is where the logic runs. An onboard module reads 64 named signals per car, 32 digital and 32 analog plus an accelerometer and GPS, and executes the operator's own fault logic table verbatim at the car. Telemetry rides the vehicle's existing cellular routers, a named mechanical desk controller owns every active fault in that territory, and alerts reach named recipient groups by severity. No training run was needed: Chronos-2 handles analog anomaly detection and seasonal trending, and a self hosted open weight reasoning model carries the work surface over the fleet ontology. Centrally it runs on one 141 GB HBM GPU class node in a contractor-hosted US cloud, about 625,000 US dollars for three years on the deepest AWS commitment in US East. A truck maker already publishes the fault codes for its vehicles; this design says where to execute them and who owns the result.

## The control networks at every site, with the evidence

Grid Context Watch is the design for the question an OT security lead and a compliance lead ask together, and a network of terminals, pipelines and automated sites asks it once per site: what is connected to the control networks, whether anything on them is behaving abnormally, and whether that can be proven with evidence when the auditor arrives. It joins 10 source systems, among them the SIEM, an OT detection tool, an IT monitoring platform, the energy management system and the substation data platform, through 2 adapter families into 14 typed objects and 14 links with the OT asset as the focal object, including the vulnerability finding, the detection rule, the pcap evidence record and the CIP evidence artefact. The boundary is read only and one way out of the control networks, and no data leaves the operator. GLM 5.2 (MIT) reasons and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Apache-2.0) retrieves, on one node of eight 141 GB HBM class GPUs; owning that node costs about 510,000 dollars over three years, about four fifths the deepest three-year AWS commitment. Every triage, case and risk acceptance carries a named OT security analyst; agents draft, the analyst decides. The paper's evidence artefacts are written for NERC CIP; a pipeline or terminal operator puts its own security directive in that place, and the shape of control networks watched one way and proven by record carries across.

## Counting what moves

Steel Count Ledger puts IP66 HDR cameras and one sealed GPU industrial PC at every installation point, counts product as it is made, and publishes the counts through a one way link into one record the authority owns. Counting survives a slow wide area link because it happens at the edge, tracker models keep one item from counting twice, and the weighbridge feed serves as acceptance ground truth. Every discrepancy case is judged by a named revenue field officer; the system counts and reconciles and never assesses, and the mill never edits a count. For a supply chain, the same pattern gives an independent count at every handover point, a dock door, a weighbridge or a gate, against what the shipping record says moved, with the detector fine tuned per product type and site as the paper describes.

## Incidents before they happen

Sovereign HSE Watch predicts health, safety and environment incidents by joining 8 systems: SAP EHS, PM and QM; SCADA; fire and gas; Vision AI cameras; SQL databases; scanned files; and the identity provider. Its 12 typed objects include the HSE incident, the near miss report, the corrective action, the sensor reading, the anomaly event and the agent recommendation, which is the shape a network of depots and terminals already keeps on paper and in separate tools, site by site. Six self hosted open weight models carry the work, including GLM 5.3 for reasoning, Chronos-2 for forecasting, RF-DETR for vision, BGE-M3 for retrieval and PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 for scans, with GLM 5.3 held at FP8 on one node of eight 141 GB HBM class GPUs (753 GB of weights, 904 GB with headroom). Every recommendation is approved or rejected by a named person, and nothing executes on equipment.

## What the records already prove

Reliability Atlas is the design to read before any sensor is bought. It joins each plant's work orders, trip history and design documents through 3 read only adapters, as exports rather than live interfaces, into a reliability object model of 13 typed objects the operator owns, among them the equipment, the failure mode, the downtime event, the criticality index and the spare part. Availability is computed by Monte Carlo simulation on reliability block diagrams built from each plant's own failure study, auditable to ISO 55000, with predictions accepted only by a named reviewer and root cause reports validated only by a named engineer. The model register is empty by design, no hardware is bought, and the study runs on the operator's own in country servers. A network with a maintenance system and years of downtime records for its cranes, conveyors, pumps and vehicles can run this study first and let it decide which of the designs above it needs second.

## What every one of them keeps constant

Across all eight, four things do not vary. The system runs on hardware the operator controls, or in a cloud or region the operator chose. A named person owns every decision, and nothing executes on equipment. The object model is published as JSON in the hyper-ontology/1 format, so a logistics operator can read the exact objects and links before building any of its own. And the cost is computed the same way in every appendix, from the paper's own sizing with every price cited, so the own or rent question has one answer per design rather than a slogan; the comparison across designs is in [Own or Rent the GPUs](https://codeatoms.ai/blog/own-or-rent-the-gpus/), and every design is listed by pattern among the [sovereign AI reference architectures](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-ai-reference-architectures/).

## What a first supply chain design would have to name

None of the eight holds a shipment, a load, a lane, a carrier, a purchase order or a delivery appointment as an object, and none reasons across two nodes at once. Terminal Pulse holds a truck visit and Port Twin holds a berth, which are the nearest shapes, but each stops at its own fence. No published design follows a load from one site to the next, or explains why a delivery that left on time arrived late. A first supply chain design adds that object model, and the join between the nodes with it. It is the design the [co-build page for supply chain and logistics](https://codeatoms.ai/co-build/supply-chain-and-logistics/) is open for: the operator brings the operation, the systems that already hold its records and one engineer who knows the network; the published designs above are the proof of what comes out.

## Use the designs

Every object model named here is in the paper's package as `ontology/objects.json`, and the same rows are in the [Vertical-Driven Architectures dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/CodeNinjatools/vertical-driven-architectures) and served live by the [codeninja-research MCP server](https://github.com/muhammadumar89/codeninja-research/tree/main/mcp-server), so a coding agent can ask which published design holds a truck visit or a fuel tank object and read why. Each paper is citable by its DOI on its page. All were reasoned on [CodeNinja Praxis](https://codeatoms.ai/praxis/) and their object models import into [Hyper Ontology](https://codeatoms.ai/hyper-ontology/).

# Physical AI System Design for Warehousing and Intralogistics: What the Published Designs Already Answer

*No warehousing design has been published in this series yet. Nine of the eighteen open reference architectures already answer the questions a warehouse or distribution center asks first: one picture of the operation from the systems it already runs, dock and yard turn time, people and vehicles seen on camera, fleet and fixed equipment condition, fire and life safety, counting what leaves, and what a records only study can settle before any sensor is bought.*

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/blog/physical-ai-system-design-for-warehousing/
Author: CodeNinja Atoms, Research distribution
Published: 2026-10-16
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja
A warehouse asks the same first questions whether it is a distribution center in the United States or a cross dock in Saudi Arabia: what is happening across the building right now in one picture, why the trucks at the dock are waiting, who is walking where the forklifts drive, which conveyor or sorter drive is about to stop, is the fire protection actually armed, and how much left the building against what the system says shipped. The series on this site holds no warehousing design yet. It holds eighteen open reference architectures in other sectors, and nine of them are written for an operation that asks one of those questions in another setting. This guide reads them as a warehouse operator would, using only what each paper says.

| Who is near the forklifts and yard vehicles | [Pit Camera Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/test-site-camera-monitoring-us/) and [Terminal Pulse](https://codeatoms.ai/truck-turn-container-terminal-us/) | A vehicle proving ground in the United States; a container terminal in the United States |

## One picture from the systems already running

Port Twin is the design to read when the problem is that every dashboard is a slice. It binds eight operational systems, five live sensor feeds and one finance backbone into a thirteen object model with the berth as the focal object, joined through three adapter families and one event backbone. The rule a warehouse will recognise is the boundary: the twin shows, and pilots, berth planners, engineers and finance staff decide in their own systems, with nothing written back into a system of record. The only model in the register is one self hosted open weight embedding model, BGE-M3, for document retrieval, about 1.1 GB of weights on virtual machines the port already runs, so no equipment is bought. For a distribution center, the warehouse management system, the transport management system, the yard system and the building's sensors take the places of the port's systems, and the dock door takes the place of the berth; the pattern of a read only twin over owned systems carries across unchanged.

## Dock and yard turn time

Terminal Pulse predicts truck turn time two hours out at a container terminal and watches the yard live. The paper's own numbers frame the problem a dock office knows: turn time averages 54 minutes and spikes above 90, and the causes live in separate systems, so planners stitch them together at the morning and afternoon operations meetings and a spike is explained hours after the trucks felt it. The design joins eleven systems, among them the terminal operating system, the gate system, two crane management systems, reefer monitoring, railroad switch lists, cameras and weather and tide feeds, into twelve objects that include the truck visit, the gate lane, the yard block and the transfer zone. Five self hosted open models carry the work: GLM 5.3 for reasoning, Chronos-2 for forecasting, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B for retrieval, and RF-DETR with Roboflow trackers for vision. Two choices transfer directly to a dock. The first rollout gate proves or redirects the yard side hypothesis using gate OCR data the operator already holds, before anything else is built. And the surfaces warn and propose while the named planner acts inside the terminal operating system; write back into that system is a second phase option gated on labour and IT sign off. The owned stack is costed at about 722,000 US dollars over three years. The operator in this paper is an illustrative scenario, not a customer.

Structure Phase Watch adds the inbound side: gate movements and delivery windows are objects in its model, read from haulage GPS, gate logs and biometric turnstiles, and every delivery window it drafts is a recommendation recorded with the approver. Its open item of 13 October is the one any camera estate on a loading apron will meet: the paper names dust, glare and heat as what degrades the lenses, and the answer recorded on its page is a cleaning rota plus a confidence drop on a fixed reference target in each camera's view that opens a work order for a named person, with the camera's health held in the object model as a record someone owns.

## People and vehicles on camera

Pit Camera Watch is a fully on premises camera system for a vehicle proving ground: 40 to 60 poles of thermal and visible camera heads, 80 to 120 streams, recorded on an N+1 pair of open source recorders holding 30 days of footage on local disk inside an isolated network. Its human rule is the conservative one a warehouse safety office may want first. Booth operators watch and decide, nothing raises an automated alarm, and only the safety office can export a clip. The one model, D-FINE under Apache-2.0 at about 8 to 124 MB of weights, searches the archive after the fact for a test vehicle, a support vehicle or a pedestrian; it is not in the live safety path. For aisles and docks, the same shape gives an investigation a searchable archive the operator owns without putting a model between a person and a near miss.

Terminal Pulse is the live counterpart. Its model holds a yard person, a transfer zone and a safety event, its detectors and trackers run in fanless enclosures at the yard blocks, gate and quay, no safety reflex crosses a network hop, and the named safety supervisor acknowledges every safety event. A warehouse choosing between the two is choosing whether the cameras search the past or watch the present, and both papers show what each choice costs in hardware and in human workload.

## Fleet faults: the operator's own logic, executed on the vehicle

Consist Watch monitors 225 commuter rail cars, and the part a forklift or tugger fleet can take is where the logic runs. An onboard module reads 64 named signals per car, 32 digital and 32 analog plus an accelerometer and GPS, and executes the operator's own fault logic table verbatim at the car. Telemetry rides the vehicle's existing cellular routers, a named mechanical desk controller owns every active fault in that territory, and alerts reach named recipient groups by severity. No training run was needed: Chronos-2 handles analog anomaly detection and seasonal trending, and a self hosted open weight reasoning model carries the work surface over the fleet ontology. A truck maker already publishes the fault codes for its vehicles; this design says where to execute them and who owns the result.

## Conveyors and sortation: advise, never trip

Turbine Island Watch reads a rehabilitated steam turbine generator through a one way path from the control system, the vibration monitoring rack and the generator protection systems. Three of its rules transfer to a conveyor drive, a sorter or a stacker crane without change. The read is one way and nothing writes to the control system. The platform advises and the protection layer trips, so every alert carries a prescribed action that a named shift operator acknowledges. And the rollout gate is a number: two false alerts per week, with thresholds tuned only on channels that have provable history. MOMENT-1 detects anomalies zero shot and no training run is needed. The compute is one 48 GB inference card on ruggedised edge servers inside the plant perimeter, costed at about 22,500 US dollars to own over three years.

## Fire and life safety, read only

Factory Fire Watch gives live visibility of fire alarm panels, fire pumps, fire water tanks and energy meters across an operator's highest risk sites, read through panel contacts, PLC inputs and LoRaWAN into an IoT platform hosted in the Kingdom, with never a write path into certified life safety equipment. No server or GPU is bought. The field equipment per site is about 2,600 to 3,200 US dollars in list prices, and a monitoring officer acknowledges or escalates every safety critical alert. The paper's framing suits a high bay building well: a sensor that has stopped reporting still reads as normal, so the design treats silence as a failure to be surfaced. For a distribution center and its sprinkler pumps, the design is the same read only estate with the sites renamed.

## Counting what leaves the building

Steel Count Ledger puts cameras and one sealed GPU industrial PC at every installation point, counts product as it is made, and publishes the counts through a one way link into one record the authority owns. Counting survives a slow wide area link because it happens at the edge, tracker models keep one item from counting twice, and the weighbridge feed serves as acceptance ground truth. The same pattern counts pallets or cases at an outbound dock door against what the warehouse management system says shipped, with the detector fine tuned per product type and site as the paper describes.

## What the records already prove

None of the nine holds a storage location, a pick face, an order line, a dock door, a forklift or a pedestrian aisle as an object, and none holds slotting: which item belongs in which location, and why. # Sensing Comes Before the Model

*Three published earth observation architectures decide what to watch from law, revisit and ownership, never from model accuracy. Two of the three ship with an empty model register.*

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/blog/sensing-comes-before-the-model/
Author: CodeNinja Atoms, Research distribution
Published: 2026-10-11
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja
The usual way to start an earth observation project is to pick the model. Someone has a segmentation network that works on satellite imagery, and the architecture grows around it.

Three designs in this corpus say the order is wrong. All three are agriculture and earth observation systems, in Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and the United States. In all three the sensing decision is made first and made from constraints that have nothing to do with accuracy: what the law allows, how often the sensor comes back, and who ends up owning the output. In two of the three, no model is committed at all.

## Two of three registers are empty, by decision

[Field Ledger](https://codeatoms.ai/farm-data-dashboard-pakistan/) is an agriculture data dashboard in Pakistan on twelve objects. Its register records zero models, and the reason is written down: the requirement commits aggregations, drill down and reporting, and no model was verified for this run. A forecaster over the sensor time series is named as open work, gated on Milestone 1 evidence rather than assumed into the design.

[Baseline](https://codeatoms.ai/vegetation-mapping-lidar-us/) is a one flight acquisition of 4 band orthoimagery and LiDAR in the United States on sixteen objects. Its register is empty too, for a blunter reason: no model layer was wanted. Vegetation analysis stays with the operator's own staff in the operator's own tools. The entry that follows it is the one most model centric designs never write, that with zero weights there is no model license to hold or to trigger, so ownership runs through the services agreement instead.

[Fodder Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/restricted-crop-monitoring-saudi-arabia/) is the only one of the three that commits models: two, on fourteen objects. A detector, RF-DETR under Apache 2.0, fine tuned per region. A forecaster, Chronos-2 under Apache 2.0, zero shot, about 120M parameters. Both licenses were part of the choice, not a footnote after it.

An empty register is a result, not a gap. It says the cross system join was the hard part and the design did not need a learned component to do it.

## What actually decided the sensing

In each design the sensing entry carries its own reason, and none of the reasons is a benchmark score.

Fodder Watch screens parcels for restricted cultivation. Its optical channel is Sentinel-2 at 10 m with a 5 day revisit, picked because it resolves center pivots for crop class without a foreign processing dependency. Its radar channel is Sentinel-1 C band SAR, and the stated reason is worth reading twice: the cloud proof complement matters because dust and haze, not cloud, are the optical channel's real attacker in that geography. Landsat 8/9 at an 8 day combined revisit is there for the archive reaching back decades, which is what gives each parcel a baseline series. The cloud layer from Sentinel-2 is recorded as evidence in the screening rule rather than as truth.

Baseline flies a manned aircraft with a 4 band red, green, blue and near infrared large format camera, because the requirement excludes unmanned data outright. Its LiDAR is a Quality Level 1 sensor at a minimum 8 pulses per square meter, with the 16 pulse option priced separately and left exercisable. The positioning entry is the one that decides whether the deliverable is QL1 at all: GNSS guidance with network RTK or an owned base station, specified by baselines, correction source and test evidence, because that chain is what the accuracy claim rests on.

Field Ledger installs no sensing whatsoever. It reads the operator's existing sensor devices, read only, no cameras, no new field hardware. The world is sensed by farm rather than watched.

Three systems in one sector, and the sensing ranges from four satellite and aerial sources to none at all. That range is the argument. Sensing is a requirements decision.

## The license is a design constraint, not paperwork

Fodder Watch has an entry that explains itself in one line: RF-DETR XL and 2XL, under Roboflow's Platform Model License, excluded. The reason is that field of use terms would compromise in Kingdom weight ownership.

That is a checkpoint rejected for its license while the smaller checkpoint under Apache 2.0 was kept. If the model had been chosen first and the sovereignty requirement read later, the design would have had to be rebuilt around a constraint it could have honored on day one.

## Where renting is not an option at any price

Fodder Watch needs one 48 GB PCIe card, L40S class, chosen by a footprint rule: the combined weights come to under 0.55 GB, which leaves batch and cache headroom. Owning that node costs about 15,200 dollars over three years, in a range of 14,600 to 15,800 once support at 8 to 12 percent a year and power at a PUE of 1.6 on the Saudi industrial tariff are counted. Renting the same card on demand in the nearest AWS region is about 60,000 dollars over the same three years, and 22,600 dollars on the deepest three year EC2 Instance Savings Plan, all upfront.

Owning wins on money here. But the line that matters in the appendix is the qualifier attached to every rental row: outside the Kingdom. For a service whose whole purpose is that detections stay sovereign, the cheapest cloud number is not a competing option. It is a measurement of what the requirement already ruled out.

## The order the designs actually follow

Read across the three and one order falls out. What the law and the operator permit you to sense. What revisit and resolution that sensing gives you. What objects those readings have to become for the question to be answerable. Only then, whether a learned model is needed at all, and only then, under what license and on whose hardware it runs.

The model is the fourth decision, and twice out of three it turns out not to be a decision at all.

---

*The three designs, their object models as JSON, their model registers and their sourced cost appendices are free to reuse under CC BY 4.0: [Field Ledger](https://codeatoms.ai/farm-data-dashboard-pakistan/), [Baseline](https://codeatoms.ai/vegetation-mapping-lidar-us/), [Fodder Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/restricted-crop-monitoring-saudi-arabia/). All three were designed on [CodeNinja Praxis](https://codeatoms.ai/praxis/) and their object models import into [Hyper Ontology](https://codeatoms.ai/hyper-ontology/). Operations are described by class, never by name.*

# The Model Register Across Sixteen Designs

*Sixteen open reference architectures for physical operations, each with a model register the operator owns outright. Twelve models, four empty registers by decision, and one licence pattern that repeats in every design.*

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/blog/the-model-register-across-sixteen-designs/
Author: CodeNinja Atoms, Research distribution
Published: 2026-10-13
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja
A model register is the part of a system design that names every learned component the operation will run, with its licence, its size and the reason it was chosen over the alternatives. Sixteen open reference architectures on this site carry one, and every row of every register is in the public dataset as `models.jsonl`. This note lines them up.

Two things stand out before the table. Four of the sixteen designs have an empty register, and in each case the emptiness is a decision the paper defends rather than a gap. And no design holds a model under a licence with a field of use restriction, a revenue trigger or a copyleft clause that would reach the operator's own code. Weight ownership is the rule the whole corpus runs on.

## The reasoning models

Five designs put a frontier class open weight model behind a work surface for the operation's own people and agents. All five chose a GLM model from the same family, self hosted at FP8 on one node of eight 141 GB HBM class GPUs, and the register says why in licence terms.

| Model | Licence | Designs that chose it | The reason the register gives |
|---|---|---|---|
| GLM 5.3, 753B mixture of experts, FP8 | Bespoke licence permitting internal commercial use with attribution and no revenue trigger | [Sovereign HSE Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-hse-pakistan/), [Steel Count Ledger](https://codeatoms.ai/steel-production-count-pakistan/), [Terminal Pulse](https://codeatoms.ai/truck-turn-container-terminal-us/) | Strongest open agentic model; purely internal use is exempt from the model as a service security review trigger; 904 GB of weights against one node of 1,128 GB leaves KV headroom |
| GLM 5.2, 753B, FP8, 1M context | MIT | [Grid Context Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/ot-security-cip-evidence-us/), [Feeder Firewatch](https://codeatoms.ai/wildfire-risk-distribution-us/) | A plain MIT licence with no revenue trigger or security review clause; one node holds it |

The split is not an accident. Where the operator wanted the strongest agentic behaviour, the design accepted a bespoke licence whose internal use carve out it had read. Where the operator was a utility or a cooperative with an auditor behind it, the design took the one generation older model under MIT and gave up nothing it needed.

## The detectors and trackers

Among the designs that watch with cameras, five chose the same detector.

| Model | Licence | Designs that chose it | The reason the register gives |
|---|---|---|---|
| RF-DETR, Nano to Large checkpoints, BF16, about 61 to 68 MB at 16 bit | Apache 2.0 | [Sovereign HSE Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-hse-pakistan/), [Steel Count Ledger](https://codeatoms.ai/steel-production-count-pakistan/), [Feeder Firewatch](https://codeatoms.ai/wildfire-risk-distribution-us/), [Terminal Pulse](https://codeatoms.ai/truck-turn-container-terminal-us/), [Fodder Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/restricted-crop-monitoring-saudi-arabia/) | The practical sovereign answer to the AGPL gate; fine tuned on the operator's own footage; the operator owns and hardens the weights. Two designs exclude the XL and 2XL checkpoints because they sit under a platform licence whose field of use terms would compromise weight ownership |
| D-FINE, N to X tiers, BF16 | Apache 2.0 | [Pit Camera Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/test-site-camera-monitoring-us/) | An unconditional licence; the N through L tiers fit one 48 GB card; ahead of DEIM on matched compute |
| Roboflow trackers, ByteTrack and OC-SORT class | Apache 2.0 | [Sovereign HSE Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-hse-pakistan/), [Structure Phase Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/structure-phase-construction-saudi-arabia/), [Steel Count Ledger](https://codeatoms.ai/steel-production-count-pakistan/) | Stable identity across frames without reintroducing copyleft after an Apache detector; one billet crossing two camera fields counts once |
| Anomalib 2.7.0, FP32, exported to ONNX Runtime | Apache 2.0 | [Hangar Form Cell](https://codeatoms.ai/dieless-sheet-metal-cell-aerospace-mro-us/) | Unsupervised fit on the facility's own good panels needs no labelled defect set |

The pattern a developer should copy is the pairing: an Apache detector followed by an Apache tracker. The register in three designs says in so many words that the tracker was chosen so that the AGPL exposure of the better known tracking collections never enters the serving path.

## The forecasters

| Model | Licence | Designs that chose it | The reason the register gives |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chronos-2, about 120M parameters, about 0.48 GB at FP32 | Apache 2.0 | [Sovereign HSE Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-hse-pakistan/), [Terminal Pulse](https://codeatoms.ai/truck-turn-container-terminal-us/), [Fodder Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/restricted-crop-monitoring-saudi-arabia/) | Zero shot multivariate forecasting with covariates and no field of use restriction; thousands of independent per parcel series with no fine tuning dependency |
| Chronos-Bolt | Apache 2.0 | [Hangar Form Cell](https://codeatoms.ai/dieless-sheet-metal-cell-aerospace-mro-us/) | Learns per arm, per stylus load baselines on the edge box and flags drifting pass signatures |
| IBM Granite Tiny Time Mixers TTM-R2, about 0.85M parameters, FP32, about 0.003 GB | Apache 2.0 | [Factory Fire Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/factory-fire-monitoring-saudi-arabia/) | A CPU only forecaster inside the operator's existing platform; the requirement asked for no server or GPU, so none was deployed |

The Granite row is the one to notice. The design covers a hundred factories and runs its forecaster on the CPU the operator already has, because a model of under a million parameters was enough and the requirement forbade buying compute.

## Retrieval and document parsing

| Model | Licence | Designs that chose it | The reason the register gives |
|---|---|---|---|
| BGE-M3, 568M parameters, FP16 | MIT | [Sovereign HSE Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-hse-pakistan/), [Port Twin](https://codeatoms.ai/port-digital-twin-us/), [Structure Phase Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/structure-phase-construction-saudi-arabia/) | Dense plus sparse plus multi vector retrieval in one pass with an 8,192 token window; multilingual retrieval across a workforce tagged by language; in the port design it is the only model in the register |
| Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, 32K window, about 1.2 GB at BF16 | Apache 2.0 | [Grid Context Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/ot-security-cip-evidence-us/), [Terminal Pulse](https://codeatoms.ai/truck-turn-container-terminal-us/) | Whole playbooks, CIP procedures or a whole shift's gate record retrieve as single passages; runs beside the frontier model |
| PaddleOCR-VL 1.6, about 0.9B parameters, BF16 | Apache 2.0 | [Sovereign HSE Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-hse-pakistan/), [Corridor Guard](https://codeatoms.ai/dc-interference-gas-pipelines-pakistan/) | Strong on degraded multilingual scans; no user or revenue threshold; digitises a scanned package with human reconciliation before any value enters the record |

The choice between the two embedders is a window question. BGE-M3 wins where the corpus is drawings, inspections and messages in several languages. Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B wins where a single document, a procedure or a shift log, must retrieve whole, and its 32K window makes that possible.

## The four empty registers

| Design | What the register says | Why |
|---|---|---|
| [Reliability Atlas](https://codeatoms.ai/plant-reliability-assessment-saudi-arabia/) | None: the register is empty by design | No inference workload is contracted; the deliverable is the study, and an empty register recorded plainly outranks a speculative entry |
| [Loop Integrity Watch](https://codeatoms.ai/tank-gauge-integrity-pakistan/) | Zero entries; all integrity logic is deterministic thresholds and rules | The failure modes are physical and protocol level, so no learned model is needed, no weights are held and no licence question arises |
| [Field Ledger](https://codeatoms.ai/farm-data-dashboard-pakistan/) | Zero models committed; a forecaster over sensor time series stays open work gated on the first milestone's evidence | The requirement commits aggregations, drill down and reporting, and no model was verified for this run |
| [Baseline](https://codeatoms.ai/vegetation-mapping-lidar-us/) | None; the register is empty by decision | No agent or model layer was wanted; analysis stays with the operator's own staff in their own tools |

A quarter of the designs needed no learned model at all. Each of those papers still carries the register, with its emptiness and the reason written down, because a reader deciding whether to copy the design needs to know that the absence was chosen.

## The licence pattern

Across the twelve named models the licences are Apache 2.0 (nine models), MIT (two) and one bespoke licence read for its internal use carve out. Three things never appear: a field of use restriction on a model the operator fine tunes, a revenue or user threshold, and a copyleft licence in the serving path. Where a stronger checkpoint existed under a platform licence, the register excludes it by name and says why.

That is the whole method. Choose the model for the job, read the licence as carefully as the benchmark, and write the reason down where the next engineer will find it.

## Use the register

The rows behind this note are the `models.jsonl` file of the [Vertical-Driven Architectures dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/CodeNinjatools/vertical-driven-architectures), one row per choice with the design, the choice, what was picked and why. The same file is served live by the [codeninja-research MCP server](https://github.com/muhammadumar89/codeninja-research/tree/main/mcp-server), so a coding agent can ask which designs chose a given model and read the reason. Every design named above was reasoned on [CodeNinja Praxis](https://codeatoms.ai/praxis/) and its object model imports into [Hyper Ontology](https://codeatoms.ai/hyper-ontology/).

## About CodeNinja

CodeNinja is a Middle Eastern-American artificial intelligence lab focused on building self-improving systems. We are reinventing knowledge work to close the loop between vertical AI use cases and the generalized intelligence that fuels it, accelerating the path toward organizational superintelligence.

# What Does It Take to Vibe Code a Truck?

*Software can now be described into existence. Physical systems cannot, because the knowledge needed to design them lives in the heads of senior engineers. This is how CodeNinja Atoms is building the missing piece: deep domain expertise for physical AI system design, carried as context instead of trained into weights.*

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/blog/what-does-it-take-to-vibe-code-a-truck/
Author: Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja
Published: 2026-10-18
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja
A year ago, vibe coding meant something new. You describe the app you want, a model writes it, you run it, you describe what is wrong, and it fixes it. A person with no training in software can now ship working software.

So here is the question I keep coming back to. What would it take to vibe code a truck?

Not the cab or the paint. The whole system. An autonomous haul truck working in a copper mine, the fleet it belongs to, the network it talks over, the people who work around it, and the regulator who has to sign it off.

Today no model can do that. This post is about why, and about what we are building at CodeNinja Atoms to change it.

## The Truck

Start with what an engineer actually has to decide before an autonomous haul truck moves a single tonne.

**Sensing.** Which lidar, radar and cameras, where they sit, and what they can see in dust, rain and at night. A sensor that works on a highway can fail on a haul road.

**Compute.** What runs on the truck, what runs at the edge of the pit, and what runs in a data center. How much power, cooling and memory each one needs, and what happens when the link drops.

**Models.** Which perception, prediction and planning models, at what size, trained or adapted on what data, and how each one is monitored once it is running.

**The site.** Haul roads, loading points, crushers, fuel bays, light vehicles driven by people, and the private network that ties them together. The truck is only safe if the site is designed around it.

**Safety and approvals.** Autonomous mining machines have their own safety standards, and each country adds its own rules on top. Someone has to write the safety case, and someone has to approve it.

**Cost and time.** What the system costs over three years, what it saves, and how long it takes before the first truck runs on its own.

**Maintenance.** How the fleet knows a part is about to fail, and who acts on it.

Every one of these decisions depends on the others. Change the sensor and the compute changes. Change the country and the approval path changes. That web of decisions is system design, and for physical AI it is one of the hardest problems there is.

## The Bottleneck

A model can write software because it has read more software than any person ever will. Billions of lines of code are public, along with the questions people asked about them and the answers that worked.

Physical system design is not like that. The knowledge sits in tender documents, internal standards, site reports and, above all, in the heads of engineers who spent twenty years in mining, oil and gas, ports or power. Very little of it is written down, and almost none of it is public.

So the bottleneck in physical AI is not the model. It is deep domain expertise. A young engineer can learn to code in a year. Learning to design a mine takes a career.

That is the problem we set out to solve. Our mission is to let a young engineer design the physical AI systems that whole industries run on, without first spending twenty years in those industries.

## CodeNinja Atoms

CodeNinja Atoms is how we work on that mission in the open. It has four parts.

**Praxis** is the platform. An engineer brings a requirement, often a real tender, and Praxis reasons out the full system design: sensing, compute, models, the object model of the operation, cost, timeline and the approvals it will need. It explains every choice, so the engineer learns the design instead of just receiving it. Praxis is free for engineers.

**Hyper Ontology** is the shared language of those designs. Every design carries an object model of the operation, the assets, people, events and rules, and how they connect, in an open JSON format called hyper-ontology/1.

**The reference architectures** are the designs we publish. There are eighteen so far, across energy, oil and gas, ports, manufacturing, agriculture, rail and more, in the United States, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Together their object models hold 246 typed objects and 228 links. They are on [codeatoms.ai](https://codeatoms.ai/sovereign-ai-reference-architectures/) and as a dataset on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/CodeNinjatools/vertical-driven-architectures).

**PADI**, the Physical AI Design Index, is the benchmark. It asks a simple question: does the Praxis platform design better systems than frontier AI on its own? It scores both on fresh tasks across 13 industries in three countries. In our latest round, a blind evaluation on seven tasks the platform had never seen, the Praxis platform passed 48.5% of the checks against 28.4% for frontier AI, and came out ahead on all seven tasks. The results are on the [PADI page](https://codeatoms.ai/padi/).

## Compression and Reinflation

The obvious way to give a model domain expertise is to fine tune it. Collect the data, train the weights, ship the model.

We chose not to, and I wrote about why in a memo, [Compression and Reinflation](https://codeatoms.ai/memos/compression-and-reinflation/). Here is the short version.

Fine tuning freezes what you know into weights. The day training ends, the world has already moved: a new regulation, a new site, a new country. And when a better model arrives, the money spent on the old weights is gone.

So we keep expertise as context instead. It works in two steps.

**Compression.** Every day, routines run over what the platform has learned: from real deals, from benchmark rounds, and from engineers correcting a design. Many observations become one sharp principle. Contradictions are resolved. What proved itself rises and what never mattered fades. What is left is small. It is not a record of everything that happened. It is the meaning of what happened.

**Reinflation.** When a new requirement arrives, say a copper mine in a country we have never worked in, no stored principle fits it exactly. It was never meant to. The model reads the compressed expertise and expands it into this site, this country's rules, this fleet and these people. The same lesson becomes a different design every time, because the world it lands in is different every time.

The idea comes from biology. The biologist Michael Levin describes memory as a bowtie: a lot of experience squeezed through a narrow middle and then expanded again for a new body and a new world. A caterpillar's lessons survive inside the butterfly, remapped for wings instead of legs.

There is one rule that makes this work. Everything is context for the model to reason over. Never a keyword match, never a lookup.

## Why It Beats Fine Tuning

Keeping expertise as context instead of weights changes four things.

**It stays current.** A new regulation is one new entry, not a new training run.

**It stays readable.** An engineer can see what the system knows, where it came from, and correct it. Nobody can read a weight.

**It survives the model.** When a stronger open weights model arrives, the expertise carries straight over and the designs improve on day one.

**It stays with the owner.** The expertise lives inside the customer's own perimeter, on their own infrastructure. For a sovereign deployment, that is the whole point.

## Back to the Truck

So what would it take to vibe code a truck?

An engineer would describe the operation: an autonomous haul fleet for a copper mine, in a named country, with a target output and a budget. The system would come back with the sensing, the compute, the models, the site network, the object model of the mine, the safety case outline, the approvals, the three year cost and the plan. Then the engineer would push back, as engineers do, and the system would explain itself and change.

That is not science fiction, and it is not finished either. It needs a model that is good at reasoning, which we now have. It needs deep domain expertise, carried in a form the model can read and an engineer can check, which is what we are building. And it needs a way to measure whether the designs are any good, which is why PADI exists.

When those three come together, the most complex physical systems in the world stop being the work of a handful of people with twenty years behind them. A young engineer anywhere can design them, and understand every choice they made.

Explore the designs, the benchmark and the platform at [codeatoms.ai](https://codeatoms.ai).

# Co-build an ontology for agriculture and earth observation

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/co-build/agriculture-and-earth-observation/
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai)
License: CC BY 4.0

Farms, irrigation and land use are watched by sensors, satellites and aircraft, but the readings, the licences and the field records usually sit in separate systems.

Recommended path: start from the nearest published agriculture and earth observation design; we extend its object model to your site.

## What we bring

- [Field Ledger: An Open Source Agriculture Data Dashboard the Operator Fully Owns](https://codeatoms.ai/farm-data-dashboard-pakistan/) (Pakistan): 12 objects, 0 models, DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23186671
- [Fodder Watch: Earth Observation That Turns Restricted-Crop Detections Into Enforceable Case Files](https://codeatoms.ai/restricted-crop-monitoring-saudi-arabia/) (Saudi Arabia): 14 objects, 2 models, DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23186675
- [Baseline: One Flight of 4 Band Orthoimagery and LiDAR for Vegetation Mapping](https://codeatoms.ai/vegetation-mapping-lidar-us/) (United States): 16 objects, 0 models, DOI https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23186673
- Praxis, the platform every design is made on: https://codeatoms.ai/praxis/
- Hyper Ontology, which stands an object model up over the operator's own systems: https://codeatoms.ai/hyper-ontology/

## What you bring

- The operation: One plant, terminal, mine, farm or network, and the outcome you want from it, in your own words. One operation, not a programme.
- The systems that already hold the records: Control systems, maintenance and ERP records, cameras, inspection sheets, whatever already exists. Nothing new has to be bought to start.
- One engineer who knows the place: Somebody who can say what an alarm really means on your site and where a number comes from.
- Where the data may sit: Your rule, not ours: in country, on your own hardware, air gapped, or in a region you name.

## What comes out

- A reference architecture for your operation: Sensing, edge, compute, the models and their licences, the sizing arithmetic and the three year cost against the alternatives.
- An object model you own: The operation written as objects and links in the hyper-ontology/1 package format, ready to load into Hyper Ontology over your own systems.
- A document your own engineers can argue with: Every number sourced, every choice stated against what it was chosen over, and the approvals and human control written down.
- Published or private, your call: Every design published on this site has the operator removed. Yours is published the same way, under CC BY 4.0, or stays private.

## Questions

### What does co-building an ontology mean?

CodeNinja Atoms designs the physical AI system for one of your agriculture and earth observation operations and writes the operation as an object model you own, in the hyper-ontology/1 package format. You bring the operation, the systems that already hold its records and one engineer who knows the site. You get the reference architecture, the object model, the sizing arithmetic and the three year cost.

### Does our data leave our country?

That is your rule, not ours. Every published design is sovereign by default: open weight models on hardware the operator owns, in country, air gapped where the operation requires it.

### Is there already a agriculture and earth observation design to read?

Yes. 3 published agriculture and earth observation reference architectures in Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and the United States, each with a DOI, an object model and a cost appendix.

Ask to co-build: https://codeatoms.ai/co-build/agriculture-and-earth-observation/#ask
Every sector: https://codeatoms.ai/co-build/

# Corridor Guard: Validated DC Interference Assessment and Mitigation for Every Gas Pipeline Near the Electrode Station

Canonical: https://codeatoms.ai/dc-interference-gas-pipelines-pakistan/
DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23308093
PDF: https://codeatoms.ai/dc-interference-gas-pipelines-pakistan/paper/corridor-guard-dc-interference-assessment-gas-pipelines-pakistan.pdf
License: CC BY 4.0
Publisher: CodeNinja Atoms (https://codeatoms.ai), a fully owned subsidiary of CodeNinja

VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · OIL & GAS · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · OCTOBER 2026

# Corridor Guard: Validated DC Interference Assessment and Mitigation for Every Gas Pipeline Near the Electrode Station

A validation-first study design that digitises, field-verifies and models the interference a high-voltage direct current electrode system imposes on the operator's transmission and distribution gas pipelines in Pakistan, and turns it into a safe-distance assessment, a priced mitigation strategy and a re-runnable model handed over on the operator's own hardware.

CodeNinja Engineering Team

For the Corrosion Control lead accountable for pipeline integrity, the cathodic protection and DC interference engineers, and the data, GIS and modelling engineers who would build and run it.

---

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja Atoms series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on CodeNinja Praxis, the CodeNinja Atoms platform for designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

At a glance

## Validated DC interference assessment for gas pipelines in Pakistan

**What this is.** An open reference architecture for system design in physical AI: a validation-first study that digitises an operator's scanned pipeline records, verifies the corridor in the field, calibrates a direct current interference model in validated software and hands the re-runnable model over on the operator's own hardware, so every safe distance ships with its evidence. It is written for the corrosion control lead accountable for pipeline integrity and for the cathodic protection, GIS and modelling engineers who would build and run it. The operator is described by class, never by name.

**The answer in numbers.**

| Part | The design |
| --- | --- |
| Sources | Two: the operator's furnished data package (alignments, coatings, soils, test points, insulating joints) and the HVDC system's stated configuration, entering through one integration adapter family |
| Object model | 15 typed objects with provenance on every attribute, from the two lines and their insulating joints through the electrode station and test points to the interference assessment and each mitigation measure, published as JSON for reuse |
| Model | PaddleOCR-VL 1.6, about 0.9 billion parameters, Apache-2.0, digitising scanned surveys with two-keyer human reconciliation; the interference physics stays in validated commercial software (CDEGS or COMSOL class) |
| Compute | One server-class host of the 48 GB PCIe inference GPU class inside the operator's estate; no field compute, no cloud, nothing crosses the boundary |
| Rollout | Three gated phases carrying 15 items: data validation, DC modelling and simulation, mitigation strategy and handover, calibrated against bipolar-baseline readings with the 1.3 kA monopolar return modelled as a conservative envelope |
| Three-year cost | About 19,500 US dollars to own the host over three years (18,700 to 20,200), about four fifths of the deepest three-year AWS commitment for one L40S card, which could not keep the data in Pakistan in any case (Appendix A) |
| Human control | A named corrosion control engineer closes every discrepancy and accepts every assessment; no value enters the register without provenance and no safe distance ships without its evidence |

**Reuse it.** The object model, the model register and the figures are free to reuse under CC BY 4.0. Cite as DOI <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23308093.>

**Made with.** Reasoned on [CodeNinja Praxis](<https://codeatoms.ai/praxis/>), the CodeNinja Atoms platform for designing physical AI systems. The object model imports into [Hyper Ontology](<https://codeatoms.ai/hyper-ontology/>), which turns it into a living system. Both are in beta; access by request.

ABSTRACT

## A Safe Distance Must Be Argued From Validated Records

The operation needs one answer argued end to end: how much direct current from a nearby high-voltage direct current electrode station shifts the pipe-to-soil potential of its transmission and distribution gas pipelines, where that shift pushes cathodic protection outside its criterion, and what mitigation with what bill of quantities restores it. It cannot be answered today because the corridor's evidence is scattered across scanned survey sheets, coating reports, layouts and soil investigations with no recorded provenance, the supplied soil figure is a single quoted value for ground the records themselves describe as layered and variable, and no calibrated interference model exists, while the governing terms make every data error the contractor's cost and release payment only after the final report.

Corridor Guard designs the work as a validation-first, three-phase study on a deliberately small stack: two named sources, the operator's own data package and the direct current system's stated configuration, entering through one integration adapter family into a governed validation register of fifteen objects with provenance carried on every attribute, served by six services and read through three surfaces, with one open-weight document parser doing the digitisation. Everything runs inside the operator's own estate on a single site-tier server: the parser turns scans into keyed values, the interference model is built and calibrated in validated commercial software against field readings, and the re-runnable model package is handed over on the operator's own hardware with no copy left outside the boundary.

The paper sets out the problem and the corridor scenario, the join failure across the supplied records, the four constraints the governing clauses impose, the stack, the fifteen-object model, ingestion through the adapter tier, inference placement inside the estate, the model and its license, the three gated phases with their item counts and exit criteria, ownership of everything the study produces, and finally how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design.
